cues.text: On Wednesday, May 23, 1447, the Blessed Sacrament was stolen from the parish church of Ettiswil, Switzerland.
Unusually for an account of this age, the theft and its aftermath were formally investigated and documented within weeks.
A young woman named Anna Vogtli, from nearby Bischoffingen, was arrested and, of her own accord, confessed fully to what she had done.
A Host Too Heavy to Carry
According to her own recorded confession, Vogtli had slipped her hand through a narrow iron gate at the church to take hold of the large consecrated Host.
Once she had passed beyond the cemetery wall, it grew so heavy in her hands that she could carry it no further and was forced to abandon it there among the nettles growing along the fence.
The abandoned Host was discovered soon afterward by a young woman named Margaret Schulmeister.
She found it lying near the churchyard fence, lifted slightly off the ground and surrounded by a vivid light.
Witnesses reported it divided into several pieces joined together, making the whole resemble a luminous flower.
The full account was compiled on July 16, 1447, by Hermann von Russeg, lord of Buron, in an official document known as the Protocol of Justice.
Produced within two months of the event itself, it is considerably more thorough than most Eucharistic traditions of this era can claim.

The recovered pieces were kept and venerated in the church at Ettiswil, and a chapel and altar built to house them were formally consecrated on December 28, 1448, roughly a year and a half after the theft.

Several popes granted indulgences to pilgrims visiting the Ettiswil shrine in the centuries that followed, and the chapel's principal feast is still kept each year on Laetare Sunday and the two days following.
The unusually well-documented civil record behind the Ettiswil account includes a named thief's own sworn confession, a dated legal protocol, and a finder identified by name.
It sets this account apart from many similar medieval traditions built largely on later retelling, giving it a documentary foundation closer to a court record than a pious legend.
